section.heading: 3.3 Cramer’s Rule, Volume, and Linear Transformations
section.paragraph: This section applies the theory of the preceding sections to obtain important theoretical formulas and a geometric interpretation of the determinant.
section.heading: Cramer’s Rule
section.paragraph: Cramer’s rule is needed in a variety of theoretical calculations. For instance, it can be used to study how the solution of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ is affected by changes in the entries of b. However, the formula is inefficient for hand calculations, except for $$2 \times 2$$ or perhaps $$3 \times 3$$ matrices.
For any $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ and any $$\mathbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , let $$A_{i}(\mathbf{b})$$ be the matrix obtained from $$A$$ by replacing column $$i$$ by the vector $$\mathbf{b}$$ .

section.paragraph: Denote the columns of $$A$$ by $$\textbf{a}_{1},\ldots \text{,} \textbf{a}_{n}$$ and the columns of the $$n \times n$$ identity matrix $$I$$ by $$\textbf{e}_{1},\ldots \text{,} \textbf{e}_{n}$$ . If $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ , the definition of matrix multiplication shows that

$$A \left(\right. I_{i} \left(\right. \mathbf{x} \left.\right) \left.\right) & = A \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\textbf{e}_{1} & \hdots & \mathbf{x} & \hdots & \textbf{e}_{n}\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}A \textbf{e}_{1} & \hdots & A \mathbf{x} & \hdots & A \textbf{e}_{n}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\textbf{a}_{1} & \hdots & \mathbf{b} & \hdots & \textbf{a}_{n}\end{matrix} \left]\right. = A_{i} \left(\right. \mathbf{b} \left.\right)$$
By the multiplicative property of determinants,
$$( \det A )(\det I_{i} ( \mathbf{x} )) = \det A_{i} ( \mathbf{b} )$$

The second determinant on the left is simply $$x_{i}$$ . (Make a cofactor expansion along the $$i$$ th row.) Hence $$(\det A) x_{i} = \det A_{i}(\mathbf{b})$$ . This proves (1) because $$A$$ is invertible and $$\det A \neq 0$$ .

section.paragraph: A number of important engineering problems, particularly in electrical engineering and control theory, can be analyzed by Laplace transforms. This approach converts an appropriate system of linear differential equations into a system of linear algebraic equations whose coefficients involve a parameter. The next example illustrates the type of algebraic system that may arise.

section.heading: A Formula for A−1
section.paragraph: Cramer’s rule leads easily to a general formula for the inverse of an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ . The $$j{th}$$ column of $$A^{- 1}$$ is a vector $$\mathbf{x}$$ that satisfies
$$A \mathbf{x} = \textbf{e}_{j}$$
where $$\textbf{e}_{j}$$ is the $$j{th}$$ column of the identity matrix, and the $$i{th}$$ entry of $$\mathbf{x}$$ is the $$(i,j) \text{-entry}$$ of $$A^{- 1}$$ . By Cramer’s rule,
$${ ( i , j ) - \text{entry of} A^{- 1} } = x_{i } = \frac{\det A_{i} ( \textbf{e}_{j} )}{\det A}$$
Recall that $$A_{ji}$$ denotes the submatrix of $$A$$ formed by deleting row $$j$$ and column $$i$$ . A cofactor expansion down column $$i$$ of $$A_{i}(\textbf{e}_{j})$$ shows that
$$\det A_{i} ( \textbf{e}_{j} ) = \left(- 1\right)^{i + j} \det A_{j i} = C_{j i}$$

where $$C_{ji}$$ is a cofactor of $$A$$ . By (2), the $$(i,j) \text{-entry}$$ of $$A^{- 1}$$ is the cofactor $$C_{ji}$$ divided by $$\text{det} A$$ . [Note that the subscripts on $$C_{ji}$$ are the reverse of $$\left( i \text{,} j \right)$$ .] Thus
$$A^{- 1} = \frac{1}{\det A} \left[\right. C_{11} & C_{21} & \ldots & C_{n 1} C_{12} & C_{22} & \ldots & C_{n 2} \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots C_{1 n} & C_{2 n} & \ldots & C_{n n} \left]\right.$$

The matrix of cofactors on the right side of (4) is called the adjugate (or classical adjoint) of $$A$$ , denoted by $$\text{adj} \textit{A}$$ . (The term adjoint also has another meaning in advanced texts on linear transformations.) The next theorem simply restates (4).

note.title: Numerical Notes
note.heading: Numerical Notes
note.paragraph: Theorem 8 is useful mainly for theoretical calculations. The formula for $$A^{- 1}$$ permits one to deduce properties of the inverse without actually calculating it. Except for special cases, the algorithm in Section 2.2 gives a much better way to compute $$A^{- 1}$$ , if the inverse is really needed.

Cramer’s rule is also a theoretical tool. It can be used to study how sensitive the solution of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ is to changes in an entry in $$\mathbf{b}$$ or in $$A$$ (perhaps due to experimental error when acquiring the entries for $$\mathbf{b}$$ or $$A$$ ). When $$A$$ is a $$3 \times 3$$ matrix with complex entries, Cramer’s rule is sometimes selected for hand computation because row reduction of $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} A & \mathbf{b} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ with complex arithmetic can be messy, and the determinants are fairly easy to compute. For a larger $$n \times n$$ matrix (real or complex), Cramer’s rule is hopelessly inefficient. Computing just one determinant takes about as much work as solving $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ by row reduction.

section.heading: Determinants as Area or Volume
section.paragraph: In the next application, we verify the geometric interpretation of determinants described in the chapter introduction. Although a general discussion of length and distance in $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ will not be given until Chapter 6, we assume here that the usual Euclidean concepts of length, area, and volume are already understood for $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ and $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ .

note.title: Theorem 9
note.heading: Theorem 9
note.paragraph: If $$A$$ is a $$2 \times 2$$ matrix, the area of the parallelogram determined by the columns of $$A$$ is $$|{\det A}|$$ . If $$A$$ is a $$3 \times 3$$ matrix, the volume of the parallelepiped determined by the columns of $$A$$ is $$|{\det A}|$$ .
﻿STUDY GUIDE provides a geometric proof of the determinant as area.

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: The theorem is obviously true for any $$2 \times 2$$ diagonal matrix:

$$\left|\right. \det \left[\right. \begin{matrix}a & 0 \\ 0 & d\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left|\right. = \left|\right. a d \left|\right. = \left{\right. \text{area of} \text{rectangle} \left.\right}$$

See Figure 1. It will suffice to show that any $$2 \times 2$$ matrix $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} \textbf{a}_{1} & \textbf{a}_{2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ can be transformed into a diagonal matrix in a way that changes neither the area of the associated parallelogram nor $$\left| \det A \middle| . \right.$$ From Section 3.2, we know that the absolute value of the determinant is unchanged when two columns are interchanged or a multiple of one column is added to another. And it is easy to see that such operations suffice to transform $$A$$ into a diagonal matrix. Column interchanges do not change the parallelogram at all. So it suffices to prove the following simple geometric observation that applies to vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ or $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ :

image.alt: A graph shows a rectangle in the first quadrant with one vertex resting on the origin.

note.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{a}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{a}_{2}$$ be nonzero vectors. Then for any scalar $$c$$ , the area of the parallelogram determined by $$\textbf{a}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{a}_{2}$$ equals the area of the parallelogram determined by $$\textbf{a}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{a}_{2} + c\textbf{a}_{1}$$ .

section.paragraph: To prove this statement, we may assume that $$\textbf{a}_{2}$$ is not a multiple of $$\textbf{a}_{1}$$ , for otherwise the two parallelograms would be degenerate and have zero area. If $$L$$ is the line through $$\textbf{0}$$ and $$\textbf{a}_{1}$$ , then $$\textbf{a}_{2} + L$$ is the line through $$\textbf{a}_{2}$$ parallel to $$L$$ , and $$\textbf{a}_{2} + c\textbf{a}_{1}$$ is on this line. See Figure 2. The points $$\textbf{a}_{2}$$ and $$\textbf{a}_{2} + c\textbf{a}_{1}$$ have the same perpendicular distance to $$L$$ . Hence the two parallelograms in Figure 2 have the same area, since they share the base from $$\textbf{0}$$ to $$\textbf{a}_{1}$$ . This completes the proof for $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ .

image.alt: The figure shows two parallel lines enclosing two parallelograms of the same area. One of the parallelograms is solid and the other one is translucent.

figure.caption: Figure 2 Two parallelograms of equal area

section.paragraph: The proof for $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ is similar. The theorem is obviously true for a $$3 \times 3$$ diagonal matrix. See Figure 3. And any $$3 \times 3$$ matrix $$A$$ can be transformed into a diagonal matrix using column operations that do not change $$|{\det A}|$$ . (Think about doing row operations on $$A^{T}$$ .) So it suffices to show that these operations do not affect the volume of the parallelepiped determined by the columns of $$A$$ .

image.alt: A figure shows a cube on a three-dimensional axis.

section.paragraph: A parallelepiped is shown in Figure 4 as a shaded box with two sloping sides. Its volume is the area of the base in the plane $$\text{Span \{} \textbf{a}_{1},\textbf{a}_{3} \text{\}}$$ times the altitude of $$\textbf{a}_{2}$$ above $$\text{Span} \{\textbf{a}_{1},\textbf{a}_{3}\}$$ . Any vector $$\textbf{a}_{2} + c\textbf{a}_{1}$$ has the same altitude because $$\textbf{a}_{2} + c\textbf{a}_{1}$$ lies in the plane $$\textbf{a}_{2} + \text{Span} \{\textbf{a}_{1},\textbf{a}_{3}\}$$ , which is parallel to $$\text{Span} \{\textbf{a}_{1},\textbf{a}_{3}\}$$ . Hence the volume of the parallelepiped is unchanged when $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} \textbf{a}_{1} & \textbf{a}_{2} & \textbf{a}_{3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ is changed to $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} \textbf{a}_{1} & {\textbf{a}_{2} + c\textbf{a}_{1}} & \textbf{a}_{3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Thus a column replacement operation does not affect the volume of the parallelepiped. Since column interchanges have no effect on the volume, the proof is complete.

figure.caption: Figure 4 Two parallelepipeds of equal volume

section.heading: Linear Transformations
section.paragraph: Determinants can be used to describe an important geometric property of linear transformations in the plane and in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . If $$T$$ is a linear transformation and $$S$$ is a set in the domain of $$T$$ , let $$T(S)$$ denote the set of images of points in $$S$$ . We are interested in how the area (or volume) of $$T(S)$$ compares with the area (or volume) of the original set $$S$$ . For convenience, when $$S$$ is a region bounded by a parallelogram, we also refer to $$S$$ as a parallelogram.

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Consider the $$2 \times 2$$ case, with $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} \textbf{a}_{1} & \textbf{a}_{2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . A parallelogram at the origin in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ determined by vectors $$\textbf{b}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{b}_{2}$$ has the form
$$S = \left{\right. s_{1} \mathbf{b}_{1} + s_{2} \mathbf{b}_{2} : 0 \leq s_{1} \leq 1 , 0 \leq s_{2} \leq 1 \left.\right}$$
The image of $$S$$ under $$T$$ consists of points of the form

$$T \left(\right. s_{1} \mathbf{b}_{1} + s_{2} \mathbf{b}_{2} \left.\right) & = s_{1} T \left(\right. \mathbf{b}_{1} \left.\right) + s_{2} T \left(\right. \mathbf{b}_{2} \left.\right) & = s_{1} A \mathbf{b}_{1} + s_{2} A \mathbf{b}_{2}$$

where $$0 \leq s_{1} \leq 1$$ , $$0 \leq s_{2} \leq 1$$ . It follows that $$T(S)$$ is the parallelogram determined by the columns of the matrix $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} {A\mathbf{b}_{1}} & {A\mathbf{b}_{2}} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . This matrix can be written as $$A B$$ , where $$B = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} \mathbf{b}_{1} & \mathbf{b}_{2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . By Theorem 9 and the product theorem for determinants,
$$\begin{matrix}{ \text{area of} T ( S )} & = \mid \det A B \mid = \mid \det A \mid \mid \det B \mid \\ & = \mid \det A \mid \cdot { \text{area of S} }\end{matrix}$$

An arbitrary parallelogram has the form $$\textbf{p} + S$$ , where $$\textbf{p}$$ is a vector and $$S$$ is a parallelogram at the origin, as seen previously. It is easy to see that $$T$$ transforms $$\textbf{p} + S$$ into $$T(\textbf{p}) + T(S)$$ . (See Exercise 26.) Since translation does not affect the area of a set,

$${ \text{area} \text{of} T ( \mathbf{p} + S )} & = & { \text{area} \text{of} T \left(\right. \mathbf{p} \left.\right) + T \left(\right. S \left.\right) \left.\right} & & & = & \left{\right. \text{area} \text{of} T \left(\right. S \left.\right) \left.\right} & & \text{Translation} & = & \mid \det A \mid \cdot { \text{area} \text{of} S } & & \text{By} \text{equation} ( \text{7} ) & = & \mid \det A \mid \cdot { \text{area} \text{of} ( \mathbf{p} + S )} & & \text{Translation}$$
This shows that (5) holds for all parallelograms in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ . The proof of (6) for the $$3 \times 3$$ case is analogous.

When we attempt to generalize Theorem 10 to a region in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ or $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ that is not bounded by straight lines or planes, we must face the problem of how to define and compute its area or volume. This is a question studied in calculus, and we shall only outline the basic idea for $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ . If $$R$$ is a planar region that has a finite area, then $$R$$ can be approximated by a grid of small squares that lie inside $$R$$ . By making the squares sufficiently small, the area of $$R$$ may be approximated as closely as desired by the sum of the areas of the small squares. See Figure 6.

image.alt: The figure consists of two parts that illustrate circles plotted on grids of varying dimensions (7 by 7 and 21 by 21), enclosing distinct regions within them.

figure.caption: Figure 6 Approximating a planar region by a union of squares. The approximation improves as the grid becomes finer

section.paragraph: If $$T$$ is a linear transformation associated with a $$2 \times 2$$ matrix $$A$$ , then the image of a planar region $$R$$ under $$T$$ is approximated by the images of the small squares inside $$R$$ . The proof of Theorem 10 shows that each such image is a parallelogram whose area is $$\text{|det} A \text{|}$$ times the area of the square. If $$R^{'}$$ is the union of the squares inside $$R$$ , then the area of $$T(R^{'})$$ is $$\text{|det} A \text{|}$$ times the area of $$R^{'}$$ . See Figure 7. Also, the area of $$T(R^{'})$$ is close to the area of $$T(R)$$ . An argument involving a limiting process may be given to justify the following generalization of Theorem 10.

figure.caption: Figure 7 Approximating T(R) by a union of parallelograms

note.paragraph: The conclusions of Theorem 10 hold whenever $$S$$ is a region in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ with finite area or a region in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ with finite volume.
